chapter: Changing styles, the road and nightlife
title: Swing bands you could dance to, each with its own identity
summary: Swing bands were rhythmic, danceable and identifiable (Miller, Dorsey, Ellington, Lunceford) until bought arrangements blurred them; Basie kept his style.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: You said you really felt that that had hurt --

Yeah, the bebop thing, yeah, right, the bebop thing. Because people -- well, Benny, when his band played, when Duke played everything, the people could dance. They were dancing, they were dancing, but they still enjoyed the music, and this is the thing.
I always preferred to hear Ellington's band up to the end play for a dance, not for a concert.

Right, right, right, because you got the full benefit of him, and you got -- and, well, Ellington, and then -- well, you had so many bands. But all of the bands were rhythmetic. Jimmy Lunceford, there's a great band.

So they were rhythmetic, everything -- and they had everything the rest of them had, had the vocals, they had the quartets, they had the whole deal going. And they had that style. And, see, the thing about bands and things then, you could hear a band and you knew who that band was. They had identity, right, so you heard with the clarinet on top, you knew that was Glenn Miller, and you knew Tommy Dorsey's sound, you know Duke Ellington's sound. And so they worked on it to an extent. But then when they started buying arrangements from various arrangers and things, then the bands kind of -- I mean, what's his name keeps his band pretty much stylized, Count Basie.
